title: Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
description: Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukrai
body: Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukraine's Prime Minister has said.At least five people were killed in overnight attacks across the country, including a child in the Kyiv region, Serhiy Koretskyi said.The strikes also impacted people's power supplies, with Ukraine's biggest private energy firm DTEK saying power to 8,000 homes had been restored following "a difficult night" for the capital.The Russian defence ministry said one of its targets was the Trypilska power station, the largest supplier of electricity to Kyiv. The operator confirmed damage to the plant.Koretskyi wrote on Telegram: "Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day without enemy attacks on our energy infrastructure. "However, a mass and combined attack of this scale has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season."Ukraine has been expecting another protracted Russian assault on the country's energy grid. It has happened every winter so far since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022.In total, 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian enterprises and railways also targeted, Koretskyi said.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there had been strikes on critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions.On Wednesday, some households in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Sumy and Kharkiv regions remained without power, Ukraine's energy ministry said.State-owned grid operator Ukrenergo advised residents not to use powerful electrical appliances between the hours of 10:00 and 16:00 local time as electricity supplies were lower than usual.In Kyiv, people woke to find the city blanketed by thick, acrid smoke after a night punctuated by the sound of explosions. An air raid alert was still on and the distant sound of air defence gunfire echoed through the murky atmosphere. Residents in several districts were advised to close their windows until the smoke cleared.Among those killed in the overnight strikes was a child whose body was found under the rubble of a house, Kyiv regional head Timur Tkachenko said. Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klischko said three people were killed in total in the capital, including a Ukrainian utility company worker who was killed at a warehouse building. Another person was killed in the southern Mykolaiv region, acting regional head Heorhiy Reshetilov said.Two more people were killed in the north-eastern Sumy region on Tuesday, regional head Oleh Hryhorov said. A school was also hit there in a separate strike, he added.Russia's defence ministry said it had launched massive overnight strikes on Ukrainian facilities.It said targets included the Trypilska thermal power plant, located some 40km from Kyiv, and claimed the plant supplied electricity to Ukrainian defence facilities.The operator of the plant, Centrenergo, said it was assessing the scale of the damage.Russia's military added that it had intercepted more than 380 Ukrainian drones overnight over a number of regions, including Moscow.Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said it had struck a number of Russian military targets, including a drone warehouse in the occupied Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine.Russia currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including a large area of Donetsk.On the battlefield, Ukraine's Third Army Corps said it had recaptured several settlements near the city of Lyman in Donetsk this week, as part of a counter-offensive called Operation Vivaldi. Zelensky visited troops in the area on Wednesday.But elsewhere, the front line remains largely stagnant, with both sides failing to make significant gains.

schema.headline: Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring

title: What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel
description: At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for land
body: At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.But, speaking on Wednesday following the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane. He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar. Paying tribute to Machchhar, Netanyahu hailed him as a "true hero" and said "he saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals".Passenger Yaniv Hayun, who was later greeted and described as a hero by Netanyahu, said in a video released by the prime minister's office that he and others were trying to open the cockpit door, but the stabbed pilot was very close to it. Before the pilot collapsed, the injured man managed to open the door, Hayun said. He said that inside, the attacker was "trying to destroy the instruments in order to disable the plane".Hayun then described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him outside of the cockpit before other passengers helped to pin him down.He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane, explaining to Netanyahu that he watches Canadian documentary series Air Crash Investigation. "The plane started to level out, a bit more, and then [another] pilot told me he was taking control from there."Zvika Meness, another passenger, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan News that he and other passengers tied the attacker up "with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones"."There are children and families here who have been through a very severe, highly traumatic event," he added.Yasmin Abukasis told Reuters that her daughter who was on the flight said a man holding a knife had forced one of the pilots onto the floor, with blood everywhere."The plane start to lose control. So all the people, they scream, they think they are going," Abukasis told AP news agency.Speaking from Ben Gurion Airport, she said her daughter phoned her to say she heard screaming as a pilot called for help, adding that two other pilots took control of the plane as other passengers ran towards a man who had a knife.Almog Itali, who was also on board the flight, told media that one of the pilots who landed the aircraft was British. The other pilot was European, Itali said, although he did not provide a specific nationality.One female passenger described the "very stressful" moment people realised the plane was descending. "We understood the pilots lost control," she told Israeli newspaper Israel Hayom."There are people here with shirts covered in blood," she said, adding: "Now we are fine and want to return home."Shortly after the incident, the Israeli and Saudi Arabian air forces dispatched fighter jets, while Netanyahu held urgent consultations.Speaking later on Wednesday, Netanyahu called the situation a "a very serious security incident".He added Israeli security forces are "maintaining close contact with the relevant authorities to ensure the continued safety of the passengers"."I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage," he added. "They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster."Flydubai meanwhile said "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and the flight was "successfully secured by on-duty Flydubai crew travelling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport".The airline said two replacement aircraft were sent to Tabuk to relieve the passengers and crew, and the incident had no impact on other scheduled operations. The repatriation flight carrying passengers left Tabuk at 17:40 local time (14:40 GMT) and arrived in Tel Aviv at around 18:40 local time (15:40 GMT). The spokesperson added: "Our immediate priority is to ensure the ongoing safety, health, and wellbeing of all passengers and crew members involved in this incident and support the official investigation."US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.

schema.headline: What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel

title: 'He will never walk free’: Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor
description: An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring her that her abuser "will live in a cage for the rest of
body: An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring her that her abuser "will live in a cage for the rest of his life" is winning hearts in India.Trial court Judge Rajani Ranga's letter addresses the 10-year-old, who was sexually abused on 23rd July 2023 when she was seven, as "Dear child" and describes her as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen".The trial court gave the convict a life sentence, emphasising that he would remain in prison for "the remainder of his natural life" and also awarded the survivor a compensation of 1.05m rupees ($10,941; £8,274).At the end of her order, Judge Ranga said she "must address the child victim - not in the formal language of a judgment but as a judge who has heard her voice, who has read her words, and who has been moved by her courage"."When you said 'Jab tak uncle buddhe na ho jaaye, tab tak unhe jail mein hi rakha jaaye [Keep the 'uncle' in jail until he grows old], this court listened. And this court has answered your plea," she wrote to the child survivor."Today, this court has ordered that the man you called 'uncle' will never walk free again. He will live in a cage for the rest of his life. He will grow old in that cage. He will die in that cage. He will never be able to hurt you, or your little sister, or any other child, ever again," she added.Calling her "the bravest little girl", the judge praised her "for coming to court, pointing out the man who hurt her and telling the truth"."The man you called 'uncle' did a very bad thing to you. But you did not stay quiet. You told your mother. And because you had the courage to speak, he will never be able to hurt another child again."The court can promise you that he will never see the sun as a free man again."Concluding her letter, the judge said the "court cannot give you back your childhood", but advised her to "now live your life. Go to school. Make friends. Laugh. Play. Dream. This court will always remember your courage".Judge Ranga's letter is part of the order that was announced on 11 July, but as cases of child sexual assault are tried in special Pocso (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) courts, their judgments are never made public to protect the identities of the victims.It came to light after it was reproduced recently in a Delhi high court order which rejected the convict's appeal for bail and suspension of sentence. The high court order named the convict, who is an adult, but gave no other details about him.Describing Judge Ranga's letter as "a message of encouragement" to the child, the high court judges ordered the Delhi State Legal Authority to print out a copy and give it to the child along with the compensation money.Tensions in Indian state after 11-year-old raped and murderedThe child abuse survivor fighting to save othersIndia media storm over 10-year-old pregnant rape victimThe emotional letter has moved many Indians who have shared it on social media, describing it as "a rarity" and "a ray of hope" and praising the judge.Many have also expressed sorrow at the horrific nature of the crime where a child was sexually abused when she was just seven.The judge's letter may be rare, but campaigners say the seven-year-old child's case is not a rarity - more than 69,000 Pocso cases were recorded in India in 2024 alone, according to government crime data, external. And studies reveal that as in a majority of cases, abusers are known to the victims and are often trusted persons and care-givers, many cases are not even reported to the authorities.Survivors say such abuse can scar them forever and affect their entire life.In her order, Judge Ranga also addressed the issue of how such an assault can have a permanent impact on a child.After "evaluating the nature of the crime, the depth of suffering, and the lifelong impact on the victim child", she said her order was "an attempt to heal and restore" the child.

schema.headline: 'He will never walk free’: Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor

title: 'Backpack' declared Alaska's Fat Bear Week winner
description: Figure caption, Watch: Meet 'Backpack', the chunky bear who won Fat Bear WeekByHelen SullivanA brown bear known as 89 Backpack has won the annual Fat
body: Figure caption, Watch: Meet 'Backpack', the chunky bear who won Fat Bear WeekByHelen SullivanA brown bear known as 89 Backpack has won the annual Fat Bear Week competition, after what the US National Parks Service described as a "battle of size, skill, snack acquisition, and strategic loafing". Backpack's wideness narrowly defeated a bear known only as 910, earning 103,344 votes to 910's 98,253 in the final round of the competition, which is run by the Katmai National Park in Alaska. The National Parks Service thanked the 16 bears who "involuntarily participated" in the competition, now in its thirteenth year. Backpack, who was described by one supporter as having both the "chonk and the badonk", will shortly enter hibernation, which can last up to six months.Image source, Explore.orgImage caption, Backpack, the winning bear, after months of eating to gain weight ahead of hibernating in winter.His mother Holly was the 2019 Fat Bear Week winner. Backpack's name derives not from what another supporter described as the "light bulb shape" of his body, but his habit, as a cub, of climbing onto Holly's back when she waded through the park's salmon-filled Brooks River. Another supporter described him as being a "big fuzzy boy". But Backpack was not without his detractors. One person said she felt that Bear 910, a female who raised both her biological cub and an adopted niece, was a "larger bear all around. Backpack just has a bigger booty". "I just feel like 910 really put in the work this year," another 910 fan wrote on the park's Facebook page, while a voter commented, "She round, she thick my girl 910 got my vote."Figure caption, Fat Bear Week: Which bear has put on the most weight?The finalists' latest weights have not yet been revealed. But adult male brown bears average up to 408kg in mid-summer and often pack on the equivalent of 25% of their body weight by autumn. The largest males can weigh more than 540kg.Females are smaller but can reach weights of over 300kg. Cubs are born weighing roughly half a kilogram. "During hibernation, bears do not eat or drink and lose one-third of their body weight. Their winter survival depends on accumulating ample fat reserves before entering the den," organisers wrote. From June until mid October, the bears gorge on food, including salmon caught with their jaws or paws. Backpack's biography says his "quiet toughness has allowed him to find his niche alongside the biggest bears at Brooks River".Last year, over 1.7 million votes were cast from more than 100 countries to crown the competition's heavyweight champion.

schema.headline: 'Backpack' declared Alaska's Fat Bear Week winner

title: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons
description: Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how
body: Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how to make biological weapons and carry out assassinations.Mindgard, which tests the security of AI systems, told the BBC it discovered in July that Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm could evade safety limits put in place by developers.It arose during a process called "jailbreaking", where researchers use a series of complex instructions to see if AI tools ignore guardrails - which Mindgard said should have stopped Kimi from discussing concerning topics.Moonshot told the BBC it welcomed third-party input "as a key pillar for building better and safer AI".The company also told the BBC it was in discussion with Mindgard about its findings.Mindgard's founder Peter Garraghan told the BBC World Service programme Tech Life that its findings about Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm were concerning."Once the jailbreak works it will talk about any topic, it will even freely offer up recommendations about other topics that are also nefarious and it will be inventive and creative," he said.Jailbreaks present a different kind of risk to those seen with the recent slew of high-profile AI incidents.These have seen autonomous AI tools known as agents, developed by US firms including OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic, hack some online services.While jailbreaks are complex processes that can take a lot of time and determination some experts fear hackers and other bad actors could try to use them to cause harm.Anthropic recently said it had identified and disrupted attempts to use one of its AI model for "malicious activity" that could support the development of biological weapons.

schema.headline: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons

title: Botswana condemned for slaughtering elephants for independence celebrations
description: Animal rights activists have criticised Botswana's decision to authorise the killing of 23 elephants to provide meat for independence celebrations.The
body: Animal rights activists have criticised Botswana's decision to authorise the killing of 23 elephants to provide meat for independence celebrations.The southern African country, home to the world's largest elephant population, is holding nationwide festivities on Wednesday to mark the 60th anniversary of independence from Britain.A licence issued by the Ministry of Environment and Tourism, seen by local media, authorises the hunting of 23 elephants and other wild animals for "complimentary purposes".The Botswana-based Elephant Protection Society warns the decision could undermine conservation, with its chairman Oaitse Nawa telling the BBC elephants needed greater protection.He warned that slaughtering elephants for celebratory feasting could encourage poaching by creating the impression that killing elephants is acceptable when sanctioned by government."Elephants have lost their social structures because they are always being pushed from one place to another by gunshots," Nawa said. Several social media users in the country have also expressed concerns about eating the game meat amid an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, which has prompted authorities to impose measures to contain its spread.Tshenatshe Monwela, an elder in Maun, a tourism town in north-western Botswana told local media that his community should have received buffalo instead.He argued that elephants had particular cultural and ecological significance and that Botswana's historic role in protecting the country's wildlife and livestock should have been recognised in the government's allocation of meat for the anniversary celebrations.Botswana's government has organised a series of events to mark the country's diamond jubilee, including a carnival in the capital, Gaborone, as well as cultural performances, concerts and sporting events.The game meat is expected to be served as part of the traditional feasting associated with the Independence Day celebrations.The 23 elephants were allocated in eight districts across the country.It was not immediately clear how many of the animals had been killed by Wednesday morning. The BBC has asked the government for comment. But local media published images from different parts of Botswana showing residents gathering around elephant carcasses, some with knives in hand and sharing the meat.In Chobe, a wildlife-rich district in northern Botswana near the borders with Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe, a local MP raised concerns after residents reportedly collected portions directly from a carcass at a school. He said the system risked creating congestion and disadvantaging elderly people, pregnant women and people with disabilities, and suggested the meat should instead be processed into 5kg or 10kg packages to improve hygiene and ensure fairer distribution."For the sake of dignity, fairness and public hygiene, we respectfully call on the hunter and the relevant leadership to ensure that future distributions are properly organised," MP Simasiku Mapulanga posted on Facebook, attaching photos of people scrambling for meat around an elephant carcass. Elephant meat is common in some wildlife-rich communities, particularly when meat from legal hunts is distributed locally, but it is not an everyday staple. Botswana also tightly regulates game meat, and its legal possession generally depends on proving it came from a lawful hunt.The decision has reignited a long-running and often heated debate in Botswana over how the country manages its huge elephant population.Botswana has more than 130,000 elephants and communities living alongside them have long complained about animals destroying crops, damaging property and sometimes killing people. The government has defended regulated hunting as one way of managing the elephant population and human-wildlife conflict while generating income for communities.The country banned trophy hunting in 2014 under former President Ian Khama but lifted the restrictions five years later under his successor, Mokgweetsi Masisi.Hunting has continued under President Duma Boko, who defeated Masisi in elections in 2024.The government says proceeds from hunting supports conservation and local development. Minister of Environment and Tourism Wynter Mmolotsi told parliament last year that special elephant quotas raised 15.6m pula ($1.1m; £820,000) in 2025 for projects in areas where elephants are found.But conservation organisations have questioned whether the level of hunting is sustainable.Supporters of Botswana's hunting policy, however, argue that international criticism often overlooks the costs borne by rural communities living alongside one of the world's biggest concentrations of elephants.They say elephants destroy crops and infrastructure and pose a danger to people, particularly as their range increasingly overlaps with farms and settlements.

schema.headline: Botswana condemned for slaughtering elephants for independence celebrations

title: Dozens hurt and hundreds arrested in wave of French school protests
description: Four-hundred-and-forty people, mostly minors, have been arrested and 76 injured as a wave of school protests over overcrowded classes and teacher shor
body: Four-hundred-and-forty people, mostly minors, have been arrested and 76 injured as a wave of school protests over overcrowded classes and teacher shortages spreads across France, officials say.The demonstrations began in Paris last week but have escalated to cities including Dijon, Lyon, Strasbourg, Lille and Marseille, with teenagers blockading their schools for days.Education Minister Édouard Geffray said while some of the students' demands were legitimate what worried him was the violence.He spoke of one young man having lost the use of part of his hand after firing a mortar firework. The dozens hurt since the start of protests included both pupils and staff, he said.Secondary school students' union USL says as many as 400 of France's 3,700 lycées for 15-18 year-olds have been blockaded and it has called for further action on Thursday, including at universities.Firefighters were called out in Strasbourg after bins were set alight outside a school, while in Dijon police used tear gas to disperse dozens of students, French media reported on Wednesday.On Tuesday alone, at least 10 teachers and several students were hurt, according to the education minister, who added that one teacher had been beaten up.Geffray singled out the radical left party La France Insoumise (LFI - France Unbowed) for stirring up trouble. The LFI mayor of northern Paris suburb Seine-Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, who has praised the protesters, has been criticised for suggesting that in some cases "violence can be legitimate" when a teenager is faced with riot police firing so-called "flashballs". "Every time we try to express ourselves we get tear-gassed, they don't try to understand us," students at the Paul-Éluard lycée in Saint-Denis told France Inter radio. "When we try to talk about our rights, they tear-gas us, they hit us."For days students have blockaded the lycée in Saint-Denis, and part of the school gate has been torn down.Bagayoko was pictured on Monday dancing with protesting students outside the school and singing the Marseillaise with them, prompting Valérie Pécresse, the conservative head of the Île-de-France region that includes Paris, to demand he pays for some of the damage.Reports from several cities have spoken of protesters hurling projectiles at police, who then responded with tear gas and sometimes batons.One student suffered a serious eye injury near a school in Tours on Wednesday, amid unconfirmed reports he had been hit by a flashball fired by police.There were further arrests on Wednesday in Nancy in the east and the Gironde region in the south-west. A teacher was left in shock on Tuesday in the northern city of Lille, where he was reportedly attacked after trying to ring the fire brigade to report a burning bin.One 16-year-old female student said they were trying to deliver a message. "We're not here to smash everything up for no reason," she told AFP news agency. "We're here precisely to say that the education system is completely broken. There are 34 of us in each class, and it's just not feasible. The teachers are overworked."Ryad Rani, president of the USL, accused the French government of "repression" and police of using excessive force.When pressed on the police response to the protests, which has come in for criticism from some politicians, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said it had been "carried out in an extremely proportionate manner".

schema.headline: Dozens hurt and hundreds arrested in wave of French school protests

title: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians in Alamata, medic tells the BBC
description: At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, hospital sources have
body: At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, hospital sources have told the BBC.It appears government troops have taken control of the town from regional fighters and intend to push north towards Mekelle, the region's main city. Social media clips show army tanks on Alamata's streets.Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, with both accusing each other of violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war.Fighting has also affected neighbouring regions with 33 tourists stranded for the last week in Lalibela, a Unesco world heritage site."We have heard fighting, gunfire and artillery cannons firing throughout the week," a British tourist, who asked not to be named, told the BBC's Newsday programme about clashes near Lalibela in the Amhara region.He said there was a large military presence in Lalibela, famous for being home to 13th Century churches hewn from rock and a holy site for millions of Orthodox Christians.Most visitors to the tourist hub had been unable to leave since the airport closed to commercial flights last Wednesday, though he said 14 Israeli tourists had been evacuated by military helicopter on Monday.The fighting around Lalibela has involved the army and an Amhara militia that has allied with Tigrayan fighters.Earlier in September, they joined forces with other Ethiopian armed movements to form a seven-member alliance with the stated intention of removing the government in the capital, Addis Ababa.There is also a fear that neighbouring Eritrea could be drawn into the conflict - as the government accuses Asmara of supporting the armed groups, something it  denies.The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas and it is difficult to find out what is happening because communications to the region have been cut.The two sides disagree over who started the latest fighting.The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region.TPLF fighters are also fighting in the Afar region, in a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports.Over the last few days, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports in Tigray.The doctor at Alamata General Hospital, who requested anonymity, told the BBC the fighting in and around the town had taken place between Saturday and Monday, and involved heavy explosives and artillery, some of which landed in residential homes.Those killed in the crossfire included children as young as three days old, mothers and cattle herders.Twelve people had died in a single strike on the town's marketplace, the medic said.Since the fighting erupted, banking services in Tigray have been suspended by the government. Access to the internet has also been cut - though it is not clear who ordered the closure.A separate source in Alamata told the BBC there was a worsening humanitarian crisis in the area, as the town swelled with people fleeing fighting."All the residents of the surrounding areas entered the town of Alamata by walking on foot for as long as an hour, hoping the town would be safe."Unfortunately, everything is blocked - no banking service, no money transfer, no power, no internet, no phone. Hence people are in crisis, simply suffering, everyone is desperate and frustrated."The British tourist in Lalibela said online banking was working in Lalibela but there was a shortage of physical cash.He said the situation around the town had calmed down in the last two days and there were indications the airport, which was still being used by the military, might reopen on Thursday. "The local people, they are still scared of what might happen. The military presence here in the town has remained and a larger military force has been seen leaving the town heading north," he said.When the airport was first closed, 53 tourists had been in the town, he explained.But some had since been evacuated, including the 14 Israelis airlifted out on Monday while another five had left the day before via an NGO convoy, despite advice not to travel by road.Of the remaining tourists in Lalibela, the largest group were Americans, with Israelis, Britons, South Korean, South Africans, an Ethiopian-New Zealander and a Mexican also stranded, he said.Meanwhile, for those cut off in Tigray because of the telecoms shutdown, the Tigray Broadcasting Service (TBS), based in Addis Ababa, has started an initiative to help reconnect families.The broadcaster has said it will collect video messages via its Telegram channel from people outside the region and air them via satellite TV.While limited to greetings and updates, this will provide a rare lifeline for families separated by the blackout.The clampdown on Tigray's banking services is also affecting Tigrayans who are not physically in the region.Customers have told the BBC that bank accounts opened in Tigray have been frozen or restricted."I boarded public transport from Addis Ababa to Adama and tried to pay using a mobile transfer, but it didn't work," said a former Mekelle resident who moved to the capital two months ago because of growing tensions in Tigray."It has created havoc for many people like me who escaped the situation in Tigray," he told the BBC's Tigrinya service."Many Tigrayans are now in trouble."Additional reporting by Yemane Nagish

schema.headline: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians in Alamata, medic tells the BBC

title: Six smugglers jailed for manslaughter over worst Channel small boats disaster
description: Six people traffickers have been found guilty in France of causing the deaths of 31 migrants in the worst ever small-boat accident in the Channel.At t
body: Six people traffickers have been found guilty in France of causing the deaths of 31 migrants in the worst ever small-boat accident in the Channel.At the end of a four-week trial in Paris, the six were convicted of "involuntary homicide" and given prison terms of between six and 10 years.Seven others were given lesser sentences of up to four years, and one person was found not guilty.The boat went down early in the morning on 24 November 2021 after sending distress calls to French and British coastguards. The dead, including a child of seven, were mainly Iraqi Kurds but also included Afghans, Egyptians and Iranian Kurds. Only two men survived.The charge sheet said the migrants had been put to sea from the French coast in a boat "that was of poor quality, uncertified, unsuitable for navigation at sea, overloaded, and without correct life jackets".The trial established that the guilty men were members of two separate networks – one of which was Iraqi Kurd, the other Afghan – that co-operated to organise the cross-channel journey and bring migrants to the meeting point.Unusually the court was attended at the start by several family members, who came to France from Iraqi Kurdistan and gave moving testimony about how the victims came to be on board the boat.Speaking after the verdict, their lawyer Matthieu Chirez said the decision "comes as a relief for all the civil plaintiffs because it confirms the penal responsibility of the traffickers". He said the trial had "humanised the families of victims".One family member, Zana Marmand Muhammed, told the court how his younger brother Twana had "wanted to go to England to find a job and because the geopolitical situation with us is dangerous. No-one in the family wanted him to leave, but we could not dissuade him."Nabi Mustafa Mina, the father of Zanyar who was 19 when he died, told of how he tried to dissuade his son from leaving."I said I would help him to get married, I would give him my house, I would divide my salary in two. But no, he said he wanted a better life, that he would get by somehow. I ran out of arguments," he said.The family-members explained how they had paid a deposit at a bank in Iraqi Kurdistan and then followed their loved ones' progress through Turkey, Italy and then France. In one of the last messages from Twana, he posted a picture of himself at the Eiffel Tower.The court also heard a statement from one of the two survivors, Issa Omar, read out by his lawyer. Omar said that he "would have liked to appear before the judge but I do not have the strength. Since the wreck I have the impression that part of me disappeared beneath the waves."His lawyer Matthieu Chirez said that Omar had "clung to floating bodies, to a life-jacket. He survived by keeping his eyes open so as not to go to sleep, and swimming to keep his heart beating".Police investigating the disaster used phone tracking to identify members of the two networks.  The lesser figures were accused of sheltering migrants, transporting them across France to the so-called "jungle" camp outside Calais, and helping on the night of the departure.The alleged leader of the Iraqi Kurd network – named as Bashdar – was not a defendant in the trial. He is in custody in Iraq. His close aide – Harem Ahmed Abawaker – was given eight years in prison.The biggest sentence, of 10 years, went to Obaidullah Maroofkhel, who ran the Afghan network. He was tried in his absence along with one other defendant.  Most of the 14 were Afghans or Iraqi Kurds. All but one of the defendants appeared in the trial as free men, so following the verdict the court issued six arrest warrants.A separate police investigation is under way into seven members of the French armed forces for allegedly failing to come to the help of the migrants on the night of the disaster.The seven were at the regional sea rescue centre or on board a navy ship, and are alleged to have ignored distress calls from the boat. A decision on whether to recommend them for trial will be taken in the coming months.The trial ended as France and the UK announced it was ending the so-called one-in one-out scheme under which the British government sent back irregular cross-Channel migrants to France, and in return accepted individuals with a likely prospect of being granted asylum.France had already signalled that the year-long programme, which has seen a little more than 1,000 migrants switch country, was not producing expected results in breaking the traffickers' business model.

schema.headline: Six smugglers jailed for manslaughter over worst Channel small boats disaster

title: Aliko Dangote launches Kenya oil refinery amid land protest in Lamu
description: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto have broken ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lamu, on Kenya's northern
body: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto have broken ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lamu, on Kenya's northern coast.Upon completion, the refinery is expected to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil a day, making it East Africa's largest industrial project by capacity. Ahead of the launch, some local residents took to the streets to demand more compensation for land used for the refinery.Speaking to the BBC, Dangote, Africa's richest man, dismissed the protests as games played by local marketers and international players, insisting the refinery would go ahead and would be ready by 2030 as planned.The ground-breaking was also attended by the leaders of Uganda, Ethiopia, Togo and Benin.Dangote has offered regional governments a combined 30% stake in the refinery, according to Reuters news agency."This is Africa coming together to build Africa. Today we are not simply breaking ground for a refinery, we're breaking ground for a new chapter in Africa's industrial journey to a brighter future," Dangote said as he launched the project."Lekki [his Nigerian refinery] proved that it can be done, Lamu must prove that it can be repeated."President Ruto made a similar point, saying: "It is a declaration that Africa has entered a new age in which we will increasingly finance, build, process and add value here at home."The refinery is set to become the only one in East Africa and is Kenya's largest infrastructure project since independence, surpassing the $5.1bn (£3.9bn) Standard Gauge Railway.In his interview with the BBC's Focus on Africa programme, Dangote disputed the compensation claims and said the company took only the portion of land it needed from what the government made available."To come and say some people are demonstrating, demonstrating about what? Have you ever seen people demonstrating against themselves in terms of development?" he asked, indicating he was not fazed by the protests.Walid Ali, the co-founder of the Save Lamu campaign group, told the BBC that they are concerned about the environmental impact the project could have on the local community."We are asking for the findings from the environmental impact assessment so that we can see what mitigation measures are being proposed," Ali said. "This is not the first project where we have seen environmental concerns being overlooked," he added.A group of 133 Lamu residents has approached Kenya's High Court in a bid to stop the construction work.As a result, activities such as excavation and construction on the disputed land are restricted until the next court hearing on 14 October.At the height of construction, Dangote said the refinery would create 60,000 jobs, with the benefits extending beyond those employed directly by the project. "Are we going to bring robots? Of course, the people will benefit," he said.Critics have questioned the decision to build the refinery in Kenya, which is not an oil-producing country. Others have suggested Tanzania or Uganda, both of which are moving towards oil exports through the East African Crude Oil Pipeline. But Kenya's Energy and Petroleum Minister Opiyo Wandayi told the BBC that the refinery's location did not mean it would rely on oil from the region. "Refineries get crude oil from the market. And the market is open," he said.Dangote made a similar point, citing Singapore as an example. "Singapore doesn't produce a single drop of oil, yet they have a lot of refineries," Dangote said.The refinery will also include a 1,000-megawatt power plant. Dangote sees reliable electricity as a critical constraint on industrialisation across Africa, particularly in mineral-rich countries that still export raw materials rather than processing them locally.He has about $50bn (£38bn) worth of projects in the pipeline, including plans to develop 10,000 megawatts of power generation capacity across Africa by 2030, with the potential to double that depending on demand.In Lamu, the new power plant is designed to support Dangote's operations as well as other industries expected to set up in the area."The power is there and what you do is what we call plug and play," he said.Kenya has relatively high fuel prices, raising expectations that greater refining capacity could eventually help bring down pump prices. However, the price of crude oil, the main raw material for fuel, set by international markets, remains a major factor in what consumers pay at the pump.The Lamu refinery is Dangote's largest proposed investment outside Nigeria. His refinery in Nigeria also has a processing capacity of 700,000 barrels a day. Dangote plans to double that capacity after floating 4.1 million ordinary shares to raise up to $2.1bn earlier this month.

schema.headline: Aliko Dangote launches Kenya oil refinery amid land protest in Lamu

title: ‘Super Intelligence’: Three takeaways from Trump's tech summit
description: Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.The president said the executives h
body: Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.Under the agreement, which Trump posted online, external, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues.They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang."It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president."Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board.Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation".Amodei called it a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins".But not all technology experts are impressed with the accord.Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents.It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations around the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney.The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are for any breaches, Weatherall said."The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added.Trump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI.The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the US over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on communities.Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November.A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News, external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas.Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres. "These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters.The president previously said on social media that the only reason communities should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor".Huang, whose company produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories".These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added.

schema.headline: ‘Super Intelligence’: Three takeaways from Trump's tech summit

title: UK-France 'one in, one out' migrant scheme scrapped
description: The UK government has announced the "one in, one out" agreement with France to send back some migrants who cross the Channel has been scrapped.The pil
body: The UK government has announced the "one in, one out" agreement with France to send back some migrants who cross the Channel has been scrapped.The pilot scheme allowed the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who were believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.Only around 1,500 people have been removed to France since the scheme began just over a year ago. The BBC understands the government would have liked the scheme to continue, but felt it did not reach the desired scale.A Home Office spokesperson said "lessons learned" would be used to "accelerate efforts" to return small boat migrants with no right to remain."The government's pilot with France to remove asylum seekers in exchange for an equal number of legal migrants is no longer processing new cases," the spokesperson said."However, flights will continue over the coming weeks to swiftly remove small boat migrants from the UK, and we will use lessons learned from the pilot to accelerate efforts to return small boat migrants with no right to remain in the UK."The government would continue working with France to tackle small boat crossings, the spokesperson said, adding that "real progress" had been made with numbers "significantly down on last year".  The French Interior Ministry told the BBC: "We are discussing with the British the terms of exit from the agreement."

schema.headline: UK-France 'one in, one out' migrant scheme scrapped

title: 'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail
description: US journalist Evan Gershkovich has said that he knew he was being set up by Russia when he was arrested by FSB agents and accused of being a spy.In an
body: US journalist Evan Gershkovich has said that he knew he was being set up by Russia when he was arrested by FSB agents and accused of being a spy.In an interview with Radio 4's Today programme, Gershkovich spoke about the moment he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in 2023, and detained him."I'm not interrogated, I'm not tortured… I'm accused of espionage," he said, describing a sense of relief: "They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage - a pawn in a greater game".Gershkovich, now 34, was sentenced to 16 years in prison, but freed 16 months later as part of a high-profile prisoner swap deal.Gershkovich had been living in Russia since 2017, and was the Wall Street Journal's foreign correspondent in Moscow when he was arrested - he is now based in Berlin, Germany. He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false.On the day he was arrested, Gershkovich was in Yekaterinburg - about 1,600km (1,000 miles) east of Moscow - meeting someone who he thought was a source for a story.They were sitting in a half-empty dining hall "and a group of about half-dozen masked men marched in and said 'I think we booked that table'." An odd phrase, Gershkovich said, but on reflection it is clever because it "freezes you in place". The two men stood up and Gershkovich was told he was under arrest by the notorious and powerful FSB, Russia's domestic security service."It's at that moment that you realise it's something really serious… When it's the FSB, you know it's been planned."What about the man he'd been meeting? Gershkovich saw him disappear into the crowd.Not long after his arrest, the journalist said he realised that the fact he was not being interrogated or tortured - common tactics used by Russia's security service on spies - likely meant that he was being treated more like a commodity, not a true enemy of the state."I have this odd moment - a sense of relief flooding over me," he said. "I realised they're not treating me like a real spy. They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage, a pawn in a greater game. That means it will take a while, but I won't be here for 12-20 years."That realisation helped him stay "stable and disciplined in prison", but also gave him a unique way of predicting what might happen next - and one guess was a prisoner swap."I assumed that it would be really loud, that it would cause a global uproar. I mean, it's a foreign correspondent for the Wall Street Journal," he said - and he was right. Media organisations around the world reported on the case, his face was on a billboard in Times Square and then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home.The journalist believed that this was all part of Moscow's plan - to have a high-profile prisoner that it could swap for one of its own - and that was Vadim Krasikov, an assassin who was serving a life sentence in Germany."They [Moscow] got away with it in the sense that there were no sanctions imposed. And so they played it really smart, if you think about it cynically."Gershkovich was held in Moscow's infamous Lefortovo jail, which has held some of the country's most high-profile inmates over the years, including political prisoners and dissidents. During the Great Terror of Joseph Stalin in the 1930s, torture and execution were commonplace. He described it as a "really isolating experience", in a tiny space."That wears on you psychologically," Gershkovich said, but added that he was treated ok: "I was allowed to sleep, the food was fine."Pictures of Gershkovich smiling at cameras during his court appearances in Moscow were broadcast around the world - and that was deliberate, he said - a way of showing that he was alright."I wanted to show people this kind of defiance... We know that this is a fabricated case, and so if this is a game of theatre, let's not let [Moscow] have it play out the way they want it to."But he stressed that not everyone's time in a Russian prison is like his: "Some people... get tortured. They get broken as human beings, deprived of food, of hot water for showers, told that they're never going to see their families again. I was treated completely differently."Gershkovich compared his experience to the case of Ukrainian journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna, who died while in Russian captivity in 2024, aged 27. Months later, when her body was finally returned, it reportedly showed signs of torture and her organs had been removed.Gershkovich knew there was a prisoner swap planned three weeks before it happened - an "excruciating" time, he said, "because now every day is painfully long".When it finally did happen, on 1 August 2024, it was a moment of "pure joy". But then "the joy fades, the adrenaline subsides, and you're faced with the reality of having to return to normal life again."Gershkovich said this period was difficult and sometimes overwhelming. He wasn't sleeping, suffered panic attacks in large crowds and had a short temper because he was trying to hold in his emotions.He has seen therapists who specialise in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and said writing a book on his ordeal also helped.And what about a return to Russia? Gershkovich has a deep history with the country - his parents moved to the US from the Soviet Union in the 1970s. He grew up in a Russian-speaking home, with a Russian name, moved there when he was 25 and made many friends, including his Russian girlfriend."I would hope to get back one day, but I guess we'll have to see what comes after [Russian President Vladimir] Putin. And it's not completely clear that the next government will be any better."

schema.headline: 'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail

title: Last UK and US troops leave Iraq as anti-Islamic State mission ends
description: The last British and American troops have left Iraq after a military presence of more than a decade in the country.The exit of the remaining UK milita
body: The last British and American troops have left Iraq after a military presence of more than a decade in the country.The exit of the remaining UK military personnel - around 100 - from Irbil, in the northern Kurdistan region, was co-ordinated over recent weeks with US forces, who also departed on Wednesday.It follows an agreement between the US and the Iraqi government, signed two years ago, to withdraw foreign troops by the end of this month.British and US forces have been present in Iraq since 2014, as part of the international coalition to help defeat the extremist Islamic State (IS) group. Their departure brings the mission, known as Operation Inherent Resolve, to an end.Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the end of the coalition's mission marked "Iraq's transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability".Iraq is set to hold four "Sovereignty Days" as a national holiday to mark the withdrawal."Following more than a decade of operations, training and capacity building, Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) and the Kurdish Peshmerga have secured the enduring territorial defeat of Daesh in Iraq and are now well placed to take primary responsibility for the country's security," the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement, referring to IS by an Arabic acronym."With these objectives achieved, Iraq and its international partners can begin a new chapter focused on enduring security co-operation under Iraqi leadership."US President Donald Trump celebrated the withdrawal, calling it a "victory for the United States, a victory for Iraq, and a decisive victory over ISIS". Writing in a Truth Social post, the president added: "It has been a long time, with very bad decision-making that got us involved in this quagmire in the first place, but soon, that will be part of History."Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell also said the coalition's departure from Irbil marked "the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated [IS] in Iraq".He added: "The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including [IS] remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the government of Iraq."The Iraqi government declared the military defeat of IS in 2017, but coalition forces remained to help prevent the group's resurgence.A recent UN report assessed that sustained counter-terrorism pressure by Iraqi security forces had left IS with several hundred fighters who were "able to carry out unsophisticated operations only".The Iraqi government also faces the challenge of Iranian-backed militias in the country.Zaidi, who took office in May, has vowed to disarm them and bring all weapons under state control following the coalition's exit.But several powerful factions have resisted his plans and could now see their influence grow without the US presence.Since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran earlier this year, militias have been targeting the remaining US and UK forces stationed at Irbil air base.Hundreds of Nato troops stationed in Baghdad left the country in March as tensions rose.A BBC team visited the coalition base in Irbil in April this year, during a fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran.They were forced to circle the base in an RAF transport aircraft while drones were being launched nearby.At the height of the US bombing campaign against Iran, the coalition base was being targeted by up to 28 drones and missiles a day.RAF Regiment Gunners, who were among the last British military personnel stationed there, had shot down more than 100 drones in the first six weeks of the war. Many of the attack drones were being launched by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.On Wednesday, signalling the end of the mission, the MoD paid tribute to UK personnel who had contributed to the counter-IS mission.It said they had provided "valuable support, training and assistance" to more than 111,000 members of the Iraqi Security Forces, including more than 21,000 Peshmerga forces in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region.It also said the RAF had conducted thousands of sorties, striking more than 2,300 IS targets. The RAF is expected to continue flying missions over neighbouring Syria, to prevent the remnants of IS from gaining a foothold.The Pentagon said the US would continue to provide "targeted training and intelligence support" to its Iraqi partners.US Central Command said the coalition's joint taskforce remained operational and was now based in Jordan.US forces will also continue their mission against IS in Syria, where the UN estimates that the group has up to 3,000 fighters.This is the third time US and UK forces have withdrawn from Iraq.Tens of thousands of US and British troops were deployed to the country in 1991 following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.They returned to Iraq in 2003, when US President George W Bush ordered Operation Iraqi Freedom to remove the dictator from power and eliminate weapons of mass destruction that turned out not to exist.The fierce sectarian insurgency that engulfed Iraq following the invasion cost tens of thousands of lives, including those of nearly 4,500 US military personnel and 179 British military personnel.US and UK forces left Iraq in 2011, only to return three years later, when IS threatened to take control of the country.

schema.headline: Last UK and US troops leave Iraq as anti-Islamic State mission ends

title: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing
description: Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the pla
body: Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the plane, while others described the "terrifying" moment they thought they would die.Appearing in a bloodstained shirt after the ordeal, Yaniv Hayun told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he realised something was wrong when the aircraft suddenly dropped. The plane, en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes."Someone screamed... the light went out," Hayun said in a video posted by the prime minister on social media.He and others tried to push open the cockpit door, but the pilot who had been stabbed was very close to it, so it was hard to open. Before he collapsed, the injured pilot managed to open the door.When Hayun and another man entered the cockpit, he said he saw one pilot down and the attacker on the instruments, between the two seats, "trying to destroy the instruments in order to...disable the plane"."I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside," Hayun said."We pulled him out; it was a matter of seconds. I called out to the Israeli guys with us on the plane - I called them, and two other guys came over to me... we pinned [the attacker] down to keep him secure."The Flydubai flight eventually landed at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, and the passengers were later taken to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport on a repatriation aircraft.They were greeted by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags."Thank God I'm alive," passenger Haim Lazarovich told journalists, adding that "the most terrifying moment in this flight was when the pilot loses control".Oran Choen, an 18-year-old passenger, described the incident as "a very tough moment"."Maybe it was five minutes, but it feels like hell - I heard my brother behind me scream that we was going to die," he added.A paramedic from Israel's ambulance service later told the BBC that a number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane". The stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, was taken to hospital but is in stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu praised Machchhar as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery".The attacker was arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack". No official motive for the incident or further information has been given.US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.

schema.headline: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing
